strengths: Clean, well-motivated design: freezing the LM and training only a lightweight adapter preserves the interpreter-subject identity and avoids the artifacts that fine-tuning introduces, a principled and clearly articulated tradeoff relative to concurrent fine-tuning approaches (LatentQA, Activation Oracles).

Conceptual reframing of existing interpretability artifacts (SAE decoder vectors with auto-interp labels; contrastive activation vectors with topic descriptions) as supervision rather than endpoints. This is a genuinely useful and reusable idea for the community.

Extensive, multi-faceted empirical evaluation across three model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5 7B-72B), multiple datasets, and multiple metrics (generation scoring, delphi detection scoring, embedding-retrieval recall@k), with careful architecture ablations (Tables 1, 7, 9, 10).

Insightful mechanistic analysis of the adapter: the bias vector accounts for ~85% of the gain (Table 1), and the ALL-CAPS (Appendix I) and zero-vector (Appendix J) experiments convincingly decompose the adapter into a 'default interpretation prior' (bias) plus semantic specificity (input vector), with scale controlling the interpolation.

Thoughtful generalization studies: cross-dataset transfer (Table 2), cross-layer pooling that matches or exceeds 32 layer-specific adapters (Table 8), and controlled experiments plus PCA (Appendix D) that isolate intrinsic dimensionality as the cause of full-rank overfitting on SAEs.

Solid reproducibility practices: full hyperparameters (Table 5), scale grids and best-of-N protocol (Appendix A.5), generation/detection scoring protocols (Appendices A.6-A.7), and compute accounting (Table 6); code and adapters are stated to be released.
Honest limitations and impact discussion (Section 5 and Impact Statement) that appropriately frames self-interpretation as partial visibility and warns about ungrounded plausible descriptions.
weaknesses: Moderate originality: learning a mapping function before injection is closely related to Tuned Lens (learned affine projections) and Patchscopes/SelfIE; the main new element is the source of supervision. The 'learned affine soft prompt' is a fairly incremental methodological step, and the paper does not perform head-to-head comparisons with concurrent fine-tuning methods (LatentQA, Activation Oracles, Li et al. 2025), which it explicitly leaves to future work.

The headline claim that trained adapters 'outperform the training labels themselves' is metric-dependent and somewhat overstated. On the independent detection-scoring metric, auto-interpretability labels achieve higher F1 (0.821) than trained adapters (0.814 SA+LR, 0.774 SA; Table 2), a fact the paper notes in passing. The advantage appears mainly on generation-scoring hit rate (Table 3: 71.4% vs 63.4% paraphrases), so the strong abstract framing should be qualified.

Potential confounds in the bridge-entity detection experiment (Section 3.5, Figure 3, Table 14): detection is defined as any generated alias appearing in any of many generations, with no false-positive control against non-bridge entities, and the alignment procedure (position 0 = first crossing of 0.001) is ad hoc. Given that the adapter is trained to emit topic names, the 91% detection rate needs stronger controls (e.g., detection of matched distractor entities) to rule out spurious entity hallucination.

Numerical inconsistencies between the abstract and body: the abstract cites '94% recall@1 versus 1%' while Section 3.2 reports 82.9% vs 0.04% and the best-of-6 figure is 93.7%; '71% vs 63%' is also reported without the metric caveat. These should be reconciled for clarity.

Potential circularity in the generation-scoring protocol, where the same model both generates test contexts and is the interpreted subject; the independent detection-scoring validation mitigates but also weakens the reported gains, and this tension is not fully resolved.

Some reproducibility gaps: the manuscript's artifact link ('We release code and trained adapters at') is missing, and the Wikipedia topic dataset and SAE sources depend on external resources (Goodfire, Llama Scope, Gemma Scope) whose versioning/label quality affects results.

Statistical framing could be stronger: the 32B anomaly in the scaling study (Figure 15) is attributed post hoc to hidden-size and layer-depth differences without a controlled test, and several comparisons rely on paired t-tests without multiple-comparison correction across the large metric/adapter grid.

strengths: The core idea is simple and practical: freeze the language model and train a lightweight adapter on existing vector-label interpretability artifacts, avoiding modification of the interpreted model. Reframing interpretability artifacts as supervision is a useful direction.

The paper reports a broad set of experiments across model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), scales (7B-72B), adapter architectures, and tasks (SAE labeling, topic retrieval, bridge-entity decoding), including cross-dataset and cross-layer generalization analyses.

Several findings are interesting and potentially useful: the scalar affine adapter with d+1 parameters is competitive; the bias vector appears to encode a generic interpretation prior; full-rank overfits on SAE features but succeeds on low-dimensional contrastive vectors; and a single cross-layer adapter can interpret activations from many layers.
Qualitative examples (e.g., held-out Goodfire latent #41101) and the ALL-CAPS/zero-vector analyses provide insight into what the adapter learns.
The impact statement and limitations discussion acknowledge partial visibility, verification concerns, and the need for complementary alignment methods.
weaknesses: Critical missing control: the paper claims the bias vector accounts for ~85% of improvement, but never reports the quantitative performance of the bias alone (f(h)=b) on generation scoring or detection scoring. Without this baseline, it is impossible to know how much of the adapter's apparent self-interpretation is input-specific versus a learned generic prior/style. This is central because a constant vector cannot interpret individual activations.

Contradictory evaluation evidence: on detection scoring, auto-interpretability labels outperform trained adapters on both Llama Scope (0.821 vs 0.814 SA+LR, 0.794 SA) and Goodfire (0.821 vs 0.772 SA+LR, 0.774 SA). The headline claim that adapters outperform training labels (71% vs 63% at 70B) rests entirely on generation scoring, which is not independently validated. The paper downplays detection scoring rather than reconciling the discrepancy.

Generation scoring is lenient and potentially gameable: it treats any nonzero activation as a hit, ignores activation magnitude and token count, and uses best-of-6 scales and multiple samples. Generic labels produced by the bias could inflate scores. The paper does not include controls such as random labels, generic labels, or bias-only outputs to rule this out.

Evaluation protocol concerns: best-of-6 scales are selected via a calibration run on a small subset, but the manuscript does not specify whether this is disjoint from evaluation, risking validation leakage. Baselines receive 6 candidates, but the comparison to LLM paraphrases and repeated labels is not clearly equivalent to the adapter's multi-scale generation.

Bridge-entity detection lacks false-positive controls. Detection is declared if any of many generated samples contains any alias of the bridge entity; the trained adapter may benefit from a generic encyclopedic prior. The paper reports no precision/control-entity analysis, so the 91% detection rate is difficult to interpret.

The scaling claim is overstated. The Taboo baseline is asserted to be a ceiling but is not formally justified; absolute performance remains below Taboo, the 32B single-layer anomaly is noted, and the monotonic trend in the averaged view is modest. 'Self-interpretation gains outpace capability gains' is not fully established.

Reproducibility and presentation: despite claiming to release code, adapters, and the Wikipedia dataset, no URLs are present. Training labels were generated by proprietary Claude Sonnet, and several references have incorrect years/keys (e.g., Cunningham et al. 2019 cited as 2023; Holtzman et al. 2025 for a 2019 paper; duplicate Li et al. 2021 entries for different works). This makes it harder to build on the work.

The conceptual framing overclaims 'self-interpretation.' The method trains an external adapter to predict labels from activations; it does not demonstrate privileged introspective access by the model itself. The frozen-model property is real, but the interpreter is still a separately trained mapping, so the distinction from prior probe/decoder approaches is smaller than presented.

strengths: The paper offers a genuinely useful conceptual reframing: interpretability artifacts (SAE decoder vectors, contrastive activation vectors) are treated as supervision rather than endpoints, and a lightweight adapter is trained while the interpreted model is fully frozen. This preserves the 'privileged access' argument better than LoRA fine-tuning of the decoder and is clearly motivated.

The empirical validation is unusually broad: multiple model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5 7B–72B), multiple SAE sources (Goodfire, Llama Scope, Gemma Scope), and multiple tasks (SAE labeling, topic retrieval, bridge-entity decoding), with cross-dataset, cross-layer, and cross-family generalization reported.

The finding that a scalar affine adapter with d+1 parameters captures most of the gain, and that the bias vector alone accounts for ~85% of the improvement, is surprising and is carefully dissected via the ALL-CAPS and zero-vector experiments, yielding a clean decomposition of prior/format (bias) versus semantics (input vector).

The bridge-entity detection result (91.0% vs 56.4% detection, 4.8x reduction in undetected entities, near-zero regression) is a compelling application demonstrating readout of implicit reasoning with no verbalized CoT.

Reproducibility is strong: code and adapters released, detailed hyperparameters, scale grids, generation/detection scoring protocols, and GPU-hour accounting are provided, and limitations and impact are discussed candidly.
Large, robust improvements over untrained SelfIE across essentially every setting (e.g., 93.7% vs ~1% recall@1 on topics; 71.4% vs 49.1% at 70B) make the core claim hard to dismiss.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'outperforming the training labels themselves' rests on generation scoring, a metric the authors define and motivate themselves, combined with a best-of-6 protocol. Under the standard detection-scoring metric (Table 2), auto-interpretability labels actually score highest (0.821 vs ~0.79), so the strongest claim is metric-dependent and not independently corroborated.

The best-of-6 comparison is not clearly neutral: the adapter draws 6 candidates from 6 different scales (high diversity), whereas the baseline draws 6 paraphrases of a single label. Best-of-N over more diverse candidates can mechanically inflate the adapter's score, which may partly explain the ~5–8 point 'beats labels' gaps. A per-candidate or single-scale comparison would be more convincing.

The decomposition shows that a constant, input-independent bias vector drives ~85% of the improvement. This raises the question of how much of the gain reflects genuine reading of the specific activation versus learning an output prior that produces plausible feature descriptions; the paper's framing as improved 'self-interpretation' is therefore somewhat stronger than what the bias-dominance result strictly supports.

The scaling claim ('self-interpretation gains outpace capability gains') is based on only four Qwen points, and the trend is metric-dependent: under single-best-layer recall@1 the 32B model breaks monotonicity (Appendix F). SelfIE also remains below the Taboo ceiling at every scale, so the 'closing gap' narrative is a projection rather than a demonstrated convergence.

The bridge-entity detection uses an ad hoc alignment procedure (position 0 defined by first crossing of a 0.001 threshold) and alias matching with a shared threshold; the aggregate heatmaps and the 91% vs 56% figures could be sensitive to these choices, and only 500 prompts are used.

Several citation inconsistencies reduce polish (e.g., 'Cunningham et al., 2019' vs '2023'; 'Karvonen et al., 2024' vs '2025'; 'Kim et al., 2024' vs '2025'; 'Holtzman et al., 2025' vs the 2019 reference; duplicated 'Li et al., 2021' entries).

strengths: Novel and clean reframing: existing interpretability artifacts (SAE decoder vectors + auto-interp labels, contrastive activation vectors + synthetic descriptions) are repurposed as (vector, label) supervision for a lightweight adapter, while the language model is kept entirely frozen. This preserves the interpreter-subject identity that fine-tuning-based approaches (LatentQA, Activation Oracles) sacrifice, and is an appealing and conceptually simple idea.

The systematic adapter-architecture study is a genuine contribution. It establishes that a scalar affine adapter with d_model+1 parameters is a strong minimal baseline, that low-rank additions help only mildly, and that full-rank transformations overfit catastrophically on SAE features but succeed on contrastive topic vectors. The intrinsic-dimensionality explanation is supported by PCA and by two controlled experiments (Wikipedia with 1 label; SAE with 6 labels) that rule out label count as a confound.

The decomposition of what the adapter learns is insightful and well-supported: the bias vector acts as an input-independent 'interpretation prior' (~85% of loss improvement), the activation vector supplies instance-specific semantics, and scale interpolates between them. The zero-vector (Appendix J) and ALL-CAPS (Appendix I) experiments provide converging evidence and are a nice use of controlled perturbations.

Empirical breadth is substantial: multiple model families (Llama-3.1/3.3, Gemma-2, Qwen-2.5), scales from 7B to 72B, two SAE families plus contrastive vectors, and four evaluation regimes (generation scoring, detection scoring, embedding retrieval, bridge-entity detection). This makes the core findings credible beyond a single setting.

The evaluation methodology shows care: a two-phase select-then-rescore protocol with independent seeds is used to avoid selection-on-noise, and the authors explicitly report that detection F1 only matches (does not exceed) the strongest baseline rather than overclaiming.

Reproducibility is relatively strong: public artifacts (Goodfire, Llama Scope, Gemma Scope SAEs; TwoHopFact), detailed hyperparameters, compute budgets, and the full data-generation prompts are provided.
weaknesses: The central 'self-interpretation' framing is in tension with the paper's own headline finding that the input-independent bias vector accounts for ~85% of the improvement. If most of the gain comes from a learned prior over the label distribution rather than from reading the specific activation, the claim that the method yields faithful interpretation of internal states is weakened; the work may be closer to a learned decoding prior than to genuine self-interpretation.

There is a self-referential evaluation risk that is not controlled. Generation scoring uses the same frozen model as both the interpreter and the substrate on which activations are measured, and the adapter is trained against labels produced by an LLM in the same family. It is not established that this does not systematically inflate trained-adapter scores relative to the auto-interp and paraphrase baselines.

The abstract headline 'outperform the training labels themselves (70% vs 50% at 70B scale)' is metric-specific (generation scoring only) and compares against the weaker of the two baselines. Against the stronger paraphrased-label baseline the margin is smaller (69.7% vs 60.4%), and on detection F1 the trained adapters only match the auto-interp baseline, so the 'outperform the labels' claim is narrower than presented.

The scaling argument (Figure 2) is plausibly confounded by a ceiling effect: the Taboo baseline approaches the retrieval ceiling (~93% to ~98% recall@100), so the reported narrowing of the gap may reflect saturation of the baseline metric rather than self-interpretation gains genuinely outpacing capability gains. The appendix partially mitigates this with recall@1/MRR but the main-text claim remains weaker than stated.

Cross-dataset generalization gains are modest (e.g., Wikipedia-trained scalar affine on SAE latents reaches 39.3% vs 30.1% for untrained SelfIE; GemmaScope-trained adapters transfer to Wikipedia at <3.5% R@1), so the transfer claims are considerably weaker than the in-distribution results and are described more strongly than the numbers warrant.

The comparison to the most relevant concurrent baseline (LoRA-based Activation Oracles) is summarized in only two sentences without full protocol, calibration, or selection details, despite being the natural point of reference for a 'comparable but frozen' claim.

Several qualitative conclusions (e.g., the SAE latent example in Table 4, the backpropagation example) rest on single cherry-picked instances, which the authors acknowledge; while illustrative, they cannot carry evidential weight and are sometimes framed as more general than they are.

strengths: The core idea is simple and useful: train lightweight activation-to-text adapters on existing interpretability artifacts (SAE feature-label pairs, contrastive topic vectors) while keeping the language model frozen. This is a clean complement to weight-modifying approaches such as LoRA-based Activation Oracles.

The empirical scope is broad: Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, and Qwen-2.5 models from 7B to 72B; multiple SAE families and a contrastive-vector dataset; cross-dataset, cross-layer, and cross-family transfer experiments.

The paper introduces a two-phase select-then-rescore evaluation protocol to mitigate selection-on-noise, and gives baselines an equal candidate budget. This is a thoughtful attempt to address a real methodological issue in best-of-N interpretability evaluations.

The bias-vector analysis is informative: zero-vector probes and ALL-CAPS training experiments support the interpretation that the bias encodes a generic format/prior while the activation vector contributes instance-specific semantics. This helps explain why a d+1 parameter scalar affine adapter is surprisingly strong.

Bridge-entity detection on TwoHopFact is a compelling application if the result holds: the adapter surfaces an intermediate entity that appears in neither prompt nor response, and outperforms untrained SelfIE and linear probes in their protocol.
The scaling experiment with a Taboo baseline makes a genuine attempt to separate self-interpretation gains from raw model capability, and the reported trend is at least suggestive.
The computational cost is modest and clearly reported, and the method requires only vector-label pairs that interpretability researchers already produce in large quantities.
The manuscript discusses limitations and impact, including the fact that self-interpretation is partial and can be misleading, which is appropriate for the topic.
weaknesses: The central reliability claim is not well supported because most headline numbers use oracle best-of-N selection. For SAE generation and detection metrics, the method selects the best of 6 candidate labels per latent using the same metric that is reported (two-phase rescoring reduces selection noise but not selection-on-ground-truth). For Wikipedia retrieval, Table 2 uses best-of-6 retrieval rank, i.e., it picks the candidate that retrieves the correct topic. In real use, the correct topic/activation score is not available to choose the scale or candidate, so the reported numbers overstate deployable performance.

The abstract claims that a scalar affine adapter with d_model+1 parameters suffices, but the strongest headline topic result (94% recall@1) is achieved by full-rank affine adapters, while scalar affine reaches only 79.4% recall@1 in Table 2. At 70B SAE scale, SA+LR is best on generation hit rate (69.7 vs 66.8 for SA). The 'suffices' claim is therefore inconsistent with the paper's own tables.

Architecture conclusions are often drawn from validation loss rather than interpretation quality. Table 1 shows SA+LR with the best validation loss, but Table 2 shows SA winning generation scoring while SA+LR ties on detection. This makes the guidance 'simpler adapters generalize better' less decisive than presented.

The bridge-entity detection result is an oracle search over layers, token positions, and many samples. Detection means that any alias appears in any generation anywhere in the layer-position grid. This demonstrates that the information is recoverable somewhere, not that the adapter reliably decodes the bridge entity at a fixed layer or position. The comparison to probes pooled across layers is similarly oracle-like.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing artifacts: the Wikipedia dataset is described as 'published at .' with no URL, no code release is provided, and a substantial part of the training data depends on proprietary Claude-generated labels. The appendix gives prompts and hyperparameters, but the central dataset and implementation remain incomplete.

The explanation for why full-rank overfits on SAE features but not on contrastive vectors—intrinsic dimensionality—is plausible but not fully established. The controlled label-count experiment is not conclusive, and Figure 9's caption admits a train-val gap while the text says there is no sign of overfitting, which is contradictory.

The scaling claim that self-interpretation gains outpace capability gains is based on a Taboo baseline that itself improves with scale and is not a perfect capability control. The 32B single-layer anomaly and the fact that SelfIE remains well below Taboo at all scales further weaken the strength of this conclusion.

The paper claims 'reliable self-interpretation,' but scale sensitivity is only partially mitigated. The adapter still requires sweeping a scale grid and selecting among candidates; no fixed-scale or scale-agnostic procedure is shown for most settings. This is a central limitation for reliability, not a peripheral one.

Generation scoring hit rate can reward generic labels that trigger any nonzero activation, and the abstract's claim that adapters 'outperform the training labels themselves' is metric-specific. Detection F1, the independent evaluation, matches but does not exceed the strongest baselines at 8B scale and is not mentioned in the abstract's headline comparison.

There is no human evaluation or independent semantic grounding beyond automatic metrics, and qualitative examples are acknowledged as cherry-picked. The 'extreme improvement' latents are a small fraction of the validation set, so their broader significance is unclear.

Presentation has several rough edges: the running header is repeated mid-page, figure captions and references are sometimes confusing, and the missing dataset URL in Appendix A.2 is a concrete omission. The abstract's numbers do not always match the tables, which makes the paper harder to trust on first read.

strengths: Well-motivated and practical framing: freezing the interpreted language model while training only a lightweight adapter on existing interpretability artifacts directly addresses the scale-sensitivity and reliability problems of untrained self-interpretation, and avoids modifying the representations being studied.

Broad and convincing empirical validation across representation types (contrastive activation vectors, Goodfire/Llama Scope/Gemma Scope SAE features), model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2.5 7B–72B), and evaluation paradigms (topic retrieval, generation/detection scoring, bridge-entity detection, scaling against a Taboo ceiling).

Large quantitative improvements are demonstrated: recall@1 on Wikipedia topics rises from ~1% for untrained SelfIE to >90% for trained adapters; at 70B scale, SAE generation scoring reaches 69.7% vs. 50.0% for auto-interpretation labels; bridge-entity detection improves from 56.4% to 91.0% on the filtered TwoHopFact set.

Insightful architectural analysis: the learned bias vector accounts for roughly 85% of the improvement, scalar affine adapters are strong and generalize well, identity-preserving low-rank variants help, and full-rank adapters overfit on SAE features but not on low-dimensional contrastive topic vectors. Controlled experiments help rule out label count as the explanation for this dichotomy.

Careful evaluation methodology: equal candidate budgets across methods, independent scoring seeds, and a two-phase select-then-rescore protocol to mitigate selection-on-noise. The paper also reports SEMs, paired t-tests, and several baselines including paraphrased auto-interp labels and LoRA Activation Oracles.

Good reproducibility and ethical treatment for a paper of this type: detailed appendices cover prompts, hyperparameters, scoring protocols, compute, and dataset construction; the impact statement acknowledges partial visibility and the risk of misleading self-descriptions rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: The headline SAE claim that trained adapters outperform the training labels themselves is metric-dependent. Adapters clearly beat auto-interp labels on generation scoring, but detection F1 ties or is close to the best baseline in some settings, so the abstract and introduction could be more precise about where the advantage holds.

Inference requires a logarithmic scale grid and per-instance selection among multiple candidate generations using the same metric later reported. Although the two-phase protocol removes selection-on-noise, this still assumes access to a scoring function and best-of-N generation at test time, which may not be available for arbitrary auditing tasks.

The scaling claim that self-interpretation gains outpace capability gains relies on a Taboo-description baseline as an imperfect proxy for all expressible knowledge. The single-layer Qwen-32B anomaly, while discussed, shows that the scaling story depends on layer pooling; stronger controls would make this claim more robust.

Novelty is real but incremental: learned affine mappings of activations are related to Tuned Lens, linear probes, and concurrent activation-oracle methods. The main contributions are the frozen lightweight-adapter setting and the empirical findings about the bias prior and architecture generalization, rather than a fundamentally new interpretability method.

The comparison to LoRA Activation Oracles is useful but limited: it uses one rank, two datasets, and does not directly test whether fine-tuning alters the representations being interpreted. The argument for freezing the model is conceptually appealing but not empirically isolated here.

Some qualitative evidence is explicitly cherry-picked, and bridge-entity detection is evaluated only on a filtered 12% subset of TwoHopFact where the model already answers both hops correctly. This limits the scope of the implicit-reasoning claim.

Reproducibility could be strengthened by clearer code and artifact links: the dataset URL appears missing or redacted in the provided manuscript, and no code repository is mentioned, which may hinder exact replication despite the detailed appendices.
